memoryReview.lesson: The geographic field and geographic orders belong to FOG; retain this source game’s specific object rather than copying its map presentation.

memoryReview.lesson: Painted restoration and the paper illustration are its central objects; this port keeps its recovered source art and its own playable control topology.

references.observation: The official play page uses colored tetromino silhouettes as the visible entry into its stacking game.
references.principle: The cell geometry itself can carry the product identity.
references.application: Retain exact square blocks and a literal vertical well with immediate movement controls.
references.avoid: Do not copy the Tetris logo, theme song or licensed trade dress.

references.observation: The playable site distinguishes solo, multiplayer and configurable key bindings around its stacker modes.
references.principle: Separate mode selection from the continuously visible playfield controls.
references.application: Preserve local and online choices while keeping one fitted shared stack during play.
references.avoid: Do not copy the competitive league, account identity or TETR.IO artwork.

references.observation: The playable page exposes soft drop, hard drop, rotation, touch controls and user-adjustable bindings.
references.principle: Every falling-piece operation must have an explicit input and understandable outcome.
references.application: Retain touch rotation and drop alongside the source configurable keyboard mappings.
references.avoid: Do not reproduce Jstris skins, support features or competitive rankings.

concepts.medium: Rebuilt Canvas 2D stacks with crisp square tiles and ghost projections; source rules and PocketNet authoritative simulation retained.
concepts.composition: A single deep-green well framed by a warm editorial shell. On phones a tiny stats strip and thumb deck surround the playable object; wide co-op wells claim the full width.
concepts.interaction: Press and hold dedicated arrows for controlled movement, tap the canvas to rotate, swipe for cellwise translation, or hit the high-contrast hard drop key.
concepts.motion: Buttons move physically by 3px on contact; gravity and score obey deterministic grid mechanics, with slight score feedback outside the board.
concepts.rationale: The original neon arcade cabinet obscured the grid at phone scale. Rebuilding the complete UI around the actual board, touch deck and network room increases legibility without replacing the working physics.

concepts.medium: A new WebGL miniature with raised physical pieces and a freely orbiting camera instead of the recovered scene renderer.
concepts.composition: An oblique miniature sits in a circular tabletop with controls represented by surrounding physical tools.
concepts.interaction: Orbit the miniature, inspect an object and manipulate it through projected three-dimensional handles.
concepts.motion: Camera inertia, object weight and spring settling would replace the source input timing and discrete presentation.
concepts.rationale: A future reinterpretation could make the object tactile, but would rebuild the renderer and make precise phone input less direct.

concepts.medium: An illustrated DOM folio with static authored state panels and short textual outcome cards.
concepts.composition: A sequence of full-screen spreads isolates one choice and one outcome at a time, with no permanently visible playfield.
concepts.interaction: Turn from a choice spread to a result spread and inspect a chronological illustrated history.
concepts.motion: Page folds and a deliberate pause between choice and result would carry the rhythm of the interaction.
concepts.rationale: A separate narrative version could explain rules slowly, but would conceal the continuously shared state needed by this recovered game.

selection.reason: Retain the existing server game and core shared board while replacing its chrome and rendering style, focused on direct touch and no scrolling during play.

rejected.reason: A new orbiting renderer would replace rather than restore the source presentation, introduce new assets and make the present direct controls less predictable.
A sequence of isolated spreads would hide simultaneous state and continuous interaction that define the source game’s playable loop.

tools.reason: The recovered browser renderer runs in local Chromium; app-local SVG install artwork is authored as editable vector geometry.

assets.role: Authored app-specific install identity accompanies the retained playable scene and appears in the page and PWA manifest.
assets.acceptance: Its concrete game motif remains distinguishable at small icon scale, without the temporary Forge monogram.
assets.integration: The PWA manifest and page icon load the local exported SVG without a CDN or network image dependency.
assets.provenance: App-specific SVG geometry authored for this restoration. Existing playable artwork remains the recovered user project content.

risks: Shared 22-column online field must fit narrow portrait without clipping adjacent controls or top iOS safe area.
Swipe gestures must never hard-drop accidentally; only the explicit hard-drop key immediately locks a piece.
On network reconnect, authoritative snapshots must not reposition the UI or lose button ownership.
comparisons: The bright paper shell and precision shared well distinguish this from FOG's geographic simulation.
Zamazka's expressive painting canvas differs from Blockies' square grid, held directional pad and read-only authoritative snapshots.
